issues.legal_issue: A payment calculated by reference to commercial sales under a conveyance that transfers less than all property rights and imposes continuing restrictions is a revenue receipt rather than repayment of capital.
material_facts: The transferor was formed to conduct cement and lime manufacture and limestone supply and acquired mining leases and related rights for those purposes.
It conveyed the benefits of leases and agreements to another company but retained some rights in the lands and imposed restrictions on the transferee.

The transferee agreed to pay an amount for each ton of cement manufactured from limestone won from the transferred lands and sold, alongside other payments linked to profits and royalties and a minimum-payment arrangement.
The deed also provided for a fixed payment and allowed termination if the limestone was exhausted.
The transferor received a payment under the per-ton covenant, which the tax authorities included in its assessable income.
issues.conclusion: The conveyance was a commercial transaction for sharing in the transferee’s commercial activities, and the payment calculated by reference to cement sold was income of a revenue nature and assessable to tax; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: For income-tax purposes, the character of a receipt is determined from the true nature of the transaction, assessed from its covenants and surrounding circumstances, rather than from the parties’ labels or the transaction’s category under general law. There is no single universal test: the court distinguishes capital repaid in instalments, as in Foley v. Fletcher, Secretary of State in Council of India v. Andrew Scoble, Oswald v. Kirkcaldy Magistrates, and Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Ramsay, from annuities and payments tied to business profits, mineral output, or sales, as illustrated by State of Bihar v. Sir Kameshwar Singh, Captain Maharajkumar Gopal Saran v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Jones v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Raja Bahadur Kamakshya Narain Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. 36149 Holdings, and Delage v. Nugget Polish Co. The court distinguished Minister of National Revenue v. Spooner, Trustees of Earl Haig v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, and Nethersole v. Withers because those cases involved different transactions or assets. The matter came to the court from a reference under section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act; the judgment identifies no separate substantive provision as the basis for classifying this receipt.

predicates.income_tax_receipt_characterization_case: An income-tax dispute concerns whether a receipt arising under a conveyance is income or capital.
predicates.payment_tied_to_commercial_sales: The transferee agreed to make a payment calculated by reference to goods made from transferred resources and sold in its business.
predicates.transferor_retained_property_rights: The transferor kept some rights in the property covered by the conveyance.
predicates.transferee_subject_to_continuing_restric: The conveyance imposed continuing restrictions on the transferee’s use or dealings with the transferred rights.

issues.definition: When an income-tax dispute concerns the character of a receipt and the payment is tied to commercial sales under a restricted transfer in which the transferor retained property rights, the receipt is revenue income assessable to tax.
